steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper studying how the choice of single-step retrosynthesis model affects multi-step synthesis planning. Explain retrosynthesis in drug discovery, the two research fields (single-step prediction and multi-step planning) with representative methods, the gap in how they are benchmarked, and what this work does.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Retrosynthesis in the DMTA cycle and computer-aided retrosynthesis
- Machine learning retrosynthesis: single-step prediction vs multi-step planning
- Single-step models: template-based and template-free
- Multi-step search algorithms
- The disconnect in how both are benchmarked
- This work

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- DMTA cycle
  - Design-Make-Test-Analyse; small molecule drug discovery; novel compounds and indications; changed by modern ML
  - retrosynthesis: core task in Make; organic chemists' synthesis planning; molecule broken into smaller subunits until easily synthesizable/purchasable; roadmap for target synthesis
  - computer-aided: save time and resources, more complex molecules, more efficient and safe routes
  - routes used by medical chemists, basis for autonomous chemistry, De Novo Drug Design synthesizability
- ML retrosynthesis
  - realignment with common ML approaches -> much larger set of candidate routes
  - two fields: single-step prediction (product -> single set of reactants) and multi-step planning (search for routes to purchasable compounds, building blocks)
- Single-step
  - supervised: predict relevant reactions and reactants
  - template-based: reaction templates abstract reaction patterns; atom and bond structures; one template covers many reactions; classification of template
    - NeuralSym (first, deep neural networks), MHNreact (information retrieval, products-templates), LocalRetro (graph, local atom and bond templates)
  - template-free: sequence-to-sequence like language translation; learn reactions, directly predict reactants; SMILES as text representation
    - Chemformer (large pretrained transformer fine-tuned), Augmented Transformer (multiple augmentation types)
  - semi-template-based: break molecule into subparts then complete into viable reactants
- Multi-step
  - search algorithms using single-step model for disconnections
  - pioneering: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) guided by a neural network at run time
  - oracle/heuristic-guided search instead of expensive run-time planning: Depth-First Proof-Number (DFPN) + neural heuristic; Retro* (A* + neural heuristic); RetroGraph (holistic graph)
  - reaction feasibility in search; synthesizability heuristics + forward synthesis model
  - self-play (success in Go): learn from prior synthesis planning runs
- Disconnect
  - single-step defines max searchable reaction network; search traverses it applying single-step's chemical info; not reflected in research
  - single-step benchmarked on one step; USPTO-50k: around 50k reactions, 10 reaction classes; not tested in multi-step search
  - multi-step benchmarked with one single-step model, often template-based NeuralSym; success rate of finding routes
  - ignores impact of alternative single-step models, though search relies on their reaction information
- This work
  - open question: are SOTA single-step methods transferable to multi-step planning, and their impact
  - plug different SOTA single-step models into a common multi-step search algorithm
  - effect on performance; relation between single-step and multi-step metrics; public and proprietary datasets, varying size and diversity
  - model suitability, chemical validity of routes

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The Design-Make-Test-Analyse (DMTA) cycle is commonly used in small molecule drug discovery to explore new compounds and indications. In recent years it has changed a lot with the introduction of modern machine-learning approaches. Retrosynthesis is a core task in the Make part of the DMTA cycle of modern drug discovery, and it is a technique that organic chemists commonly use in synthesis planning. A molecule is broken down step by step into smaller subunits until easily synthesizable or purchasable compounds are reached, and the overall goal is to produce a roadmap for synthesizing a target compound. With computer-aided retrosynthesis, researchers in chemistry and in machine learning want to accelerate the development of chemical synthesis by saving time and resources, by addressing more complex molecules or by producing more efficient and safe routes. The generated routes can be used by medical chemists to create molecules of interest, they can be a basis for autonomous chemistry, or they can be used in De Novo Drug Design to assess synthesizability.

The core advance in retrosynthesis was the realignment with common machine learning approaches, which lets users consider a much larger set of possible synthesis routes. The machine learning field of retrosynthesis prediction is usually split into two research fields, called single-step retrosynthesis prediction and multi-step synthesis planning. Single-step retrosynthesis prediction means breaking down a product into a single set of reactants, and multi-step synthesis planning means the search algorithms that are used to find synthesis routes that lead to purchasable compounds (building blocks).

More specifically, single-step retrosynthesis prediction is a supervised learning task, made to predict which reactions are relevant to a target molecule and the reactants that are needed to produce that reaction. There are two commonly referenced categories of single-step retrosynthesis models, template-based and template-free. Template-based methods use reaction templates, which are an abstraction of the reactions in the data that summarize the underlying pattern of these reactions. There are different ways of extracting templates, but in all cases the aim is to represent the atom and bond structures needed to perform a reaction, and a single template represents multiple reactions. Template-based methods treat single-step prediction as a classification problem where the task is to predict the right template for the target molecule/product. Examples of template-based methods are NeuralSym, the first approach in the field, which showed that deep neural networks are useful for retrosynthesis prediction, MHNreact, which uses an information retrieval approach to associate products and templates, and LocalRetro, which uses a graph representation to predict relevant local atom and bond templates for the product.

Template-free approaches, on the other hand, usually treat retrosynthesis prediction as a sequence-to-sequence prediction problem, and they use methods from natural language processing like language translation tasks. Instead of extracting and predicting the templates, they try to learn the underlying reactions so they can predict the reactants directly. Product and reactants are usually given as Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES), which is a common text-based representation of chemical entities. Examples of template-free methods are Chemformer, a large pretrained transformer model that is fine-tuned on the retrosynthesis task, and Augmented Transformer, a transformer architecture that uses multiple types of augmentation. There are other variations of these approaches, like semi-template-based methods where the molecule is first broken down into subparts and then completed to produce chemically viable reactants.

- Multi-step planning: search algorithms using a single-step model for disconnections
  - MCTS guided by neural network at run time (pioneering)
  - oracle/heuristics instead: DFPN + neural heuristic; Retro* (A* + neural heuristic); RetroGraph (holistic graph)
  - reaction feasibility; synthesizability heuristics + forward model; self-play (Go) from prior runs
- Intertwined: single-step defines searchable network; not reflected in research
- Benchmarks: USPTO-50k, around 50k reactions, 10 reaction classes; no multi-step testing; multi-step uses one single-step model (often NeuralSym)
- This work: SOTA single-step models in a common multi-step search; single-step vs multi-step metrics; public and proprietary data; model suitability, chemical validity

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:

The machine learning field of retrosynthesis prediction is usually split into two research fields, called single-step retrosynthesis prediction and multi-step synthesis planning. There are different ways of extracting templates, but in all cases the aim is to represent the atom and bond structures needed to perform a reaction, and a single template represents multiple reactions. Template-based methods treat single-step prediction as a classification problem where the task is to predict the right template for the target molecule/product. Examples of template-based methods are NeuralSym, the first approach in the field, which showed that deep neural networks are useful for retrosynthesis prediction, MHNreact, which uses an information retrieval approach to associate products and templates, and LocalRetro, which uses a graph representation to predict relevant local atom and bond templates for the product.

Template-free approaches, on the other hand, usually treat retrosynthesis prediction as a sequence-to-sequence prediction problem, and they use methods from natural language processing like language translation tasks. Instead of extracting and predicting the templates, they try to learn the underlying reactions so they can predict the reactants directly. Product and reactants are usually given as Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES), which is a common text-based representation of chemical entities. Examples of template-free methods are Chemformer, a large pretrained transformer model that is fine-tuned on the retrosynthesis task, and Augmented Transformer, a transformer architecture that uses multiple types of augmentation. There are other variations of these approaches, like semi-template-based methods where the molecule is first broken down into subparts and then completed to produce chemically viable reactants.

Multi-step synthesis planning is about researching new synthesis route search algorithms that use a single-step model to find retrosynthetic disconnections. The pioneering approach in the field uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to plan the traversal of the search tree at run time, guided by a neural network. Other route planning algorithms use an oracle function or heuristics to guide the tree search, instead of relying on run time planning which is compute-expensive. Prominent examples are Depth-First Proof-Number (DFPN), which combines classical DFPN with a neural heuristic, Retro*, which combines A* pathfinding with a neural heuristic, or RetroGraph, which applies a holistic graph-based approach. Other approaches include reaction feasibility in the tree search or use synthesizability heuristics together with a forward synthesis model. Lastly, self-play approaches, motivated by how successful they were in Go, learn to guide the tree search by using information gathered from earlier runs of synthesis planning.

Single-step retrosynthesis prediction and multi-step synthesis planning are inherently intertwined: the single-step method defines the maximum reaction network that can be searched, and the search algorithm tries to traverse this network efficiently by repeatedly applying the chemical information stored in the single-step model. But this connection is not reflected in current research.

Right now, single-step methods are benchmarked by predicting a single retrosynthetic step from a product to reactants. The common benchmark data for these methods, USPTO-50k, has around 50k reactions and only a limited diversity of 10 reaction classes. These methods are usually only tested on reactant prediction and not inside multi-step search algorithms, so their usability for synthesis planning is not assessed. In the same way, multi-step search algorithms benchmark the route-finding capabilities of their method with a single single-step model, often based on the template-based NeuralSym model, and they evaluate the success rate of finding possible synthesis routes for molecules of interest. However, using only one single-step model does not consider the impact of alternative single-step models, which is a vital aspect of the search, because the route planning algorithm uses the reaction information stored in the single-step model to find synthesis routes and to create alternate reaction pathways in the reaction network.

The question that remains is whether state-of-the-art single-step retrosynthesis methods are transferable to the multi-step synthesis planning domain, and what their impact on multi-step synthesis planning is. In this work, we address the transfer between single-step and multi-step methods by putting different state-of-the-art single-step models into a common multi-step search algorithm and analyzing how these models can be used for multi-step synthesis planning. We explore the effect on performance, and we analyze the relationship between contemporary single-step and multi-step performance metrics using both public and proprietary datasets of different size and diversity. We also focus on vital aspects like model suitability and the chemical validity of the predicted routes.

steps.text:
The Design-Make-Test-Analyse (DMTA) cycle is commonly used in small molecule drug discovery to explore novel compounds and indications. Over recent years, it has seen massive changes with the introduction of modern machine-learning approaches [1]. Retrosynthesis, a core task in the Make part of the DMTA cycle of modern drug discovery, is a technique commonly used by organic chemists in synthesis planning: a molecule is successively broken down into smaller subunits until easily synthesizable or purchasable compounds are obtained [2,3], with the overall goal of producing a roadmap for the synthesis of a target compound. With computer-aided retrosynthesis, researchers in both chemistry and machine learning aim to accelerate the development of chemical synthesis by saving time and resources, addressing more complex molecules or producing more efficient and safe routes. These generated routes can be used by medical chemists to create molecules of interest [4], serve as a basis for autonomous chemistry [5], or be incorporated into De Novo Drug Design to assess synthesizability [6].

The core advance in retrosynthesis has been the realignment with common machine learning approaches [7], which allows users to consider a much larger set of potential synthesis routes. The machine learning field of retrosynthesis prediction is commonly separated into two research fields, referred to as single-step retrosynthesis prediction and multi-step synthesis planning. Single-step retrosynthesis prediction refers to breaking down a product into a single set of reactants, while multi-step synthesis planning refers to the search algorithms used to find synthesis routes leading to purchasable compounds (building blocks).

Specifically, single-step retrosynthesis prediction is a supervised learning task, developed to predict which reactions are relevant to a target molecule and the corresponding reactants required to produce this reaction. There are two commonly referenced categories of single-step retrosynthesis models, template-based and template-free [7]. Template-based methods use reaction templates, an abstraction of the reactions in the data which summarizes the underlying pattern of these reactions. There are different approaches to extracting templates, though in all cases they aim to represent the atom and bond structures required to perform a reaction [8], with a single template representing multiple reactions. Template-based methods consider single-step prediction as a classification problem where the task is to predict the appropriate template for the target molecule/product. Examples include NeuralSym [9], the first approach in the field, which demonstrated the usefulness of deep neural networks for retrosynthesis prediction, MHNreact [10], which uses an information retrieval approach to associate products and templates, and LocalRetro [11], which uses a graph representation to predict relevant local atom and bond templates for the product.

On the other hand, template-free approaches commonly treat retrosynthesis prediction as a sequence-to-sequence prediction problem [8], employing methods seen in natural language processing such as language translation. Instead of extracting and predicting the corresponding templates, these approaches aim to learn the underlying reactions to directly predict reactants. Product and reactants are typically represented as Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES), a common text-based representation of chemical entities. Examples of template-free methods include Chemformer [12], a large pretrained transformer model fine-tuned on the retrosynthesis task, and Augmented Transformer [13], a transformer architecture which employs multiple types of augmentation. Other variations of these approaches exist, such as semi-template-based methods where the molecule is first broken down into subparts and then completed to produce chemically viable reactants [14,15,16].

Multi-step synthesis planning focuses on novel synthesis route search algorithms that use a single-step model to identify retrosynthetic disconnections. The pioneering approach in the field uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to plan the traversal of the search tree at run time, guided by a neural network [2]. Alternative route planning algorithms use an oracle function or heuristics to guide the tree search instead of relying on compute-expensive run time planning. Prominent examples are Depth-First Proof-Number (DFPN) [17], which combines classical DFPN with a neural heuristic, Retro*, which combines A* pathfinding with a neural heuristic [18], and RetroGraph, which applies a holistic graph-based approach [19]. Other approaches incorporate reaction feasibility into the tree search [20] or use synthesizability heuristics in combination with a forward synthesis model [21,22]. Finally, self-play approaches, motivated by their success in Go [23], learn to guide the tree search by leveraging information gathered from prior runs of synthesis planning [24,25,26].

Single-step retrosynthesis prediction and multi-step synthesis planning are inherently intertwined: the single-step method defines the maximum searchable reaction network, and the search algorithm tries to traverse this network efficiently by repeatedly applying the chemical information stored in the single-step model. However, this connection is not reflected in contemporary research.

Currently, single-step methods are benchmarked by predicting a single retrosynthetic step from a product to reactants. The common benchmark data for these methods, USPTO-50k [27,28], consists of around 50k reactions and has only a limited diversity of 10 reaction classes. These methods are typically tested only on reactant prediction and not within multi-step search algorithms, so their usability for synthesis planning is not assessed. Similarly, multi-step search algorithms benchmark their route-finding capabilities using a single single-step model, often the template-based NeuralSym model [2,26,19,17,18], and evaluate the success rate of finding potential synthesis routes for molecules of interest. However, using only one single-step model ignores the impact of alternative single-step models, a vital aspect of the search, since the route planning algorithm uses the reaction information stored in the single-step model to find synthesis routes and create alternate reaction pathways within the reaction network.

The question remains whether state-of-the-art single-step retrosynthesis methods are transferable to the multi-step synthesis planning domain, and what their impact on multi-step synthesis planning is [29,30]. In this work, we address the transfer between single-step and multi-step methods by incorporating different state-of-the-art single-step models within a common multi-step search algorithm to analyze the use of these models for multi-step synthesis planning. We explore the effect on performance, analyzing the relationship between contemporary single-step and multi-step performance metrics using both public and proprietary datasets of varying size and diversity. Moreover, we focus on vital aspects such as model suitability and the chemical validity of the predicted routes.
